title: Computing continuous sky view factors using 3D urban raster and vector databases: comparison and application to urban climate
relevance_reason: The term 'vector databases' in this paper refers to GIS vector data (geometric features such as buildings and roads) versus raster data, not to vector databases used for similarity or nearest-neighbor search. The paper's subject is urban climatology and SVF computation, with no discussion of vector indexing, similarity search, or vector database systems.
research_focus: Computing continuous sky view factors (SVF) using 3D urban raster and GIS vector databases, comparing the two approaches, and evaluating the relationship between urban geometry (quantified by SVF) and intra-urban nocturnal temperature variations in Szeged, Hungary.
method: Two methods are applied and compared: a vector-based algorithm and a raster-based digital elevation model (DEM) approach for computing continuous SVF images over the urban area. Areal means of SVF and temperature difference (ΔT) are then related to assess the SVF–urban heat island relationship.
application_domain: Urban climatology and urban heat island (UHI) studies
results_summary: The paper compared a vector-based and a raster-based method for computing continuous sky view factors over the urban area of Szeged, Hungary. Both methods produced very similar SVF values (r² = 0.9827), confirming their mutual validity for describing urban geometry. The raster-based method was significantly faster (38 hours versus 12 days for the vector-based method), while the vector-based method could capture small SVF values near building walls more accurately. The study confirmed that urban surface geometry, quantified by SVF, is a significant determining factor of intra-urban nocturnal air temperature distribution. The usefulness of applying areal means in SVF–temperature relations, as suggested by Unger (2004, 2007), was validated.
limitations: Conversion from vector to raster format results in loss of information; Data accessibility: datasets that include building heights are still rare; Computation time of the shadow casting algorithm increases quadratically as the number of pixels increases; If large areas are to be studied, image resolution must be decreased to speed up computation

title: Assessing the relationship between sky view factor and land surface temperature to the spatial resolution
relevance_reason: The paper is about urban heat island effect, sky view factor, and land surface temperature at different spatial resolutions; the 'vector database' mentioned is a GIS vector database storing 3D building geometry, not a vector database for similarity or nearest-neighbor search, and no vector database technology is discussed.
research_focus: The dependence of the relationship between sky view factor (SVF) and land surface temperature (LST) on spatial resolution, in the context of assessing the urban heat island effect and urban morphology.
method: Multi-resolution thermal imagery (Landsat 8 TIRS, ASTER, TASI-600) was used to retrieve LST, while a 3D building vector database (GIS) was used to compute SVF maps at matching spatial resolutions. Weighted linear regression analyses were then performed to assess the SVF-LST correlation across different resolutions and sensors.
application_domain: Urban climate, urban heat island analysis, and remote sensing of urban morphology
results_summary: The paper demonstrates a positive relationship between daytime LST and SVF across all three sensor types, consistent with existing literature. For same-sensor images at different dates, the regression trends are nearly superimposable, indicating stable relationships. However, significant differences in regression coefficients appear when comparing data from different sensors, attributed to the different spatial resolutions affecting SVF values. At fine resolution, micro-scale factors (building materials, anthropogenic heat, humidity) introduce variability, while at coarser resolutions these are smoothed out. The authors conclude that the minimum resolution element should be no less than 30 m and that the optimal spatial resolution depends on the specific application scale.
limitations: The lack of reliable cartographic digital data can be a limiting factor when airborne thermal data are used; The optimal spatial resolution cannot be univocally determined and must be tuned to the specific application; Micro-scale factors (thermal properties of building materials, anthropogenic heat, humidity, pollutants) interfere with SVF and LST values at fine resolutions
research_gaps: Studies on how spatial resolution affects the LST-SVF relationship were missing in the literature prior to this work; The definition of optimal spatial resolution is usually related to the smallest object of interest, but this approach cannot always be easily followed when it is difficult to identify a reference sample

title: Change detection of buildings from satellite imagery and lidar data
relevance_reason: The paper is about geospatial change detection using SVM, satellite imagery, and lidar data. The 'vector database' mentioned refers to a traditional GIS cartographic database storing geometric features (polygons, lines), not a vector database for high-dimensional similarity search. No vector indexing or nearest neighbor search technology is addressed.
research_focus: Automatic detection of building changes (new constructions, demolitions, and planimetric inaccuracies) by comparing SPOT5 satellite imagery and lidar data with existing vector cartographic databases for topographic map updating.
method: Support vector machine (SVM) classification applied to a joint dataset of SPOT5 multispectral satellite imagery and lidar-derived digital surface models, with automatic training derived from the existing vector cartographic database. Results are visualized using a traffic-light map for human operator review.
application_domain: Cartography and geospatial change detection (building extraction and map updating at 1:25,000 scale)
results_summary: The paper proposes an SVM-based semi-automatic method for detecting building changes between satellite/lidar data and existing vector cartographic databases. The method achieves 98% accuracy in identifying new and demolished buildings in the study area of Alcalá, Spain. SPOT5 imagery with two infrared bands proved more effective than higher-resolution RGB aerial imagery for discriminating buildings from vegetation. Small buildings surrounded by tall trees and structures with unusual spectral signatures (e.g., purple tile roofs) remain difficult to detect. The method is scalable via tiling and suitable for industrial cartographic production environments.
limitations: Small houses and low buildings surrounded by high trees present significant detection problems; DTM errors from lidar processing can create false positives (e.g., steep hills mistaken for buildings); Buildings with unusual spectral signatures (e.g., purple tile roofs) may be missed as false negatives; Bridges on highways are falsely detected as buildings due to their height in the DSM; The method can only detect buildings with ground plant size greater than 2.5 m × 2.5 m due to SPOT5 resolution; Incoherencies in the original vector cartographic coding (e.g., wrong building codes) propagate into the results
research_gaps: Future use of RGB plus near-infrared aerial images combined with lidar could improve detection of smaller buildings; The method would need modifications to apply to new data types planned by the Spanish NMA

title: The Influence of Sky View Factor on Daytime and Nighttime Urban Land Surface Temperature in Different Spatial-Temporal Scales: A Case Study of Beijing
relevance_reason: The 'building vector database' referenced in this paper is a GIS vector data source storing building geometries, not a vector database for similarity search or nearest neighbor search. The paper's subject is urban thermal environment analysis using remote sensing, with no discussion of vector indexing, ANN, or vector database technology.
research_focus: The relationship between sky view factor (SVF) and land surface temperature (LST) at different spatial and temporal scales in the core built-up area of Beijing, including seasonal variation, day-night variation, and the impact of building height and density.
method: SVF was calculated using a geometric method based on a building vector database (GIS vector data), and LST was retrieved from Landsat-8 and ASTER thermal infrared remote sensing imagery. The SVF-LST relationship was then analyzed across four periods in 2018, at 30 m and 90 m pixel scales, and across three building height categories (low-rise, mid-rise, multi-story).
application_domain: Urban thermal environment and remote sensing (urban morphology, land surface temperature analysis)
results_summary: The study found that SVF and LST are positively correlated at night, while the daytime relationship varies depending on image scale and season. Nonlinear fitting of the SVF-LST relationship was better at 30 m scale than at 90 m scale. The average building shadow ratio was largest in winter, particularly in mid-rise building areas, and the cooling effect of shading influenced the SVF-LST relationship. At 90 m scale, fitting results were more consistent across building scenes, whereas at 30 m scale the relationship differed by building height category. The authors concluded that factors beyond building morphology, such as vegetation, water bodies, and anthropogenic heat, also affect LST distribution.
limitations: Vegetation and water interference were ignored during statistical analysis; Only SVF and building shadow ratio were used to analyze the influence of 3D building structure on LST; The influence of different building functions producing different anthropogenic heat was not considered
research_gaps: Further studies should consider the influence of the joint building functional area and the surrounding environment on land surface temperature

title: Automated Image-to-Map Discrepancy Detection using Iterative Trimming
relevance_reason: The paper uses 'vector database' in the GIS sense (a database of geographic vector features such as forest polygons) and is fundamentally about remote sensing change detection; it has no connection to vector similarity search, nearest neighbor search, or vector indexing technology (HNSW, IVF, etc.).
research_focus: Detecting discrepancies between existing cartographic vector databases (GIS maps) and more recent remote sensing images to automate forest map updating, specifically for detecting clear cuts and regeneration in forest stands.
method: An automated workflow combining geographic object-based image analysis (multi-resolution segmentation with median filtering) to label image segments based on the GIS database, followed by non-parametric statistical iterative trimming to identify outliers (discrepancies) using a likelihood threshold (alpha parameter).
application_domain: Forest map updating and remote sensing change detection
results_summary: The paper designed an automated workflow to compare a forest GIS map with a more recent satellite image without interactive training sample selection. Geographic object-based image analysis provided automatically labeled image segments after matching the GIS database to the image. Statistical iterative trimming then detected discrepancies as outliers, achieving about 75% detection of forest regeneration and 100% detection of clear cuts with less than 10% commission errors. The method's sensitivity was tunable via the alpha parameter, with optimal values varying between deciduous and coniferous stands. The overall approach was shown to be flexible and promising for diverse applications, though limited to relatively small proportions of change.
limitations: The method is limited by construction to relatively small percentages (10-20%) of discrepancies between remote sensing data and the map; The segmentation algorithm is a bottleneck because composite objects mislead edge delineation or embed small changed areas inside forest stands; Red and NIR wavelengths proved not appropriate for detecting deciduous forest within coniferous objects due to similar reflectance values; The optimal alpha value requires user tuning and cannot be extrapolated from a single case study; Small objects such as small buildings or linear elements were not properly detected due to inappropriate spatial resolution
research_gaps: Further work is necessary to classify the discrepancy type using existing classification algorithms trained by automatically selected samples; Decision rules must be developed to assimilate the change information into the vector database; An optimized workflow for other land-cover types should include a step for selecting the most meaningful characteristics (e.g., texture or shape) to discriminate each class

title: Selecting appropriate variables for detecting grassland to cropland changes using high resolution satellite data
relevance_reason: The 'vector database' (LPIS) referenced in this paper is a GIS spatial database storing land parcel polygon geometries, not a vector database for similarity search or nearest neighbor search. The paper is entirely about remote sensing-based land cover change detection and has no connection to vector indexing, ANN search, or vector database technology.
research_focus: Identifying the most suitable remote sensing variables (spectral, textural, temporal) for detecting grassland-to-cropland land cover change using a pair of Landsat 8 OLI images and the Land Parcel Identification System (LPIS) as reference data.
method: Generalised Linear Models (GLM) were fitted using 59 candidate variables derived from Landsat 8 imagery (vegetation indices, Tasselled Cap components, PCA, textures). Model quality was verified through multi-temporal object-based change detection against the LPIS reference database.
application_domain: Land Use and Land Cover (LULC) change detection, remote sensing, agricultural land monitoring
results_summary: The paper tested 59 variables in GLM-based models for grassland-to-cropland change detection and found that a three-variable model combining NDVI, Wetness, and the Fifth Tasselled Cap component provides the best practical accuracy-interpretability trade-off. Increasing the number of variables beyond three did not significantly improve detection accuracy and instead complicated interpretation. The best raw accuracy was achieved using the original Landsat 8 bands directly rather than derived variables. The results are considered applicable for landscape management, agriculture, and subsidy policy in Central Europe with similar environmental conditions.
limitations: LPIS reference data may contain errors because land use information is entered directly by farmers; LPIS data refers to the end of the year rather than the exact satellite acquisition date; Results are limited to areas with similar geographical and environmental conditions in Central Europe; Selection of suitable image pairs was constrained by cloud cover and the 2013 satellite launch date
research_gaps: Further research is needed to combine the selected variables with spatial data acquired by other remote sensing techniques (e.g., radar/Sentinel-1, thermal/Landsat 8 TIRS, time series, very high resolution data)

title: A model-based approach for automatic building database updating from high-resolution space imagery
relevance_reason: The paper concerns GIS building database updating from satellite imagery; the 'vector database' referenced is a GIS vector data store for building geometries, not a vector database for similarity search or nearest neighbor retrieval. No vector indexing, similarity search, or vector database technology in the modern sense is discussed.
research_focus: Automatic updating of building boundaries in a GIS vector database from high-resolution satellite imagery using SVM classification and model-based matching against existing building shapes
method: Binary SVM classification of pan-sharpened IKONOS imagery augmented with nDSM and NDVI bands to detect building patches, followed by model-based delineation where shape parameters (area, perimeter, major/minor axis, elongation, compactness, solidity) are used to select the best-matching building from the existing GIS database and rotate it to fit the detected patch
application_domain: GIS database updating and building extraction from satellite imagery
results_summary: The approach was tested in the Batikent district of Ankara, Turkey, using IKONOS imagery and an existing 1:1000-scale building database. SVM classification achieved 92.45% overall accuracy and a kappa coefficient of 0.8490 for building patch detection. Delineation of 108 out of 111 new buildings succeeded, yielding 97.30% accuracy, with building detection percentage values of 80.54–92.09% and quality percentage values of 66.37–84.77% across 14 test areas. The approach successfully handled complex shapes (S, C, H) by selecting models from the existing database rather than requiring a predefined model library. Failures occurred for buildings smaller than 50 m² and when similarly shaped buildings led to erroneous model selection.
limitations: Buildings smaller than 50 m² could not be delineated because small patches were removed as artefacts; Closely spaced buildings could be detected as a single joined building; Buildings with similar shape parameters in the existing database could lead to erroneous model selection; Newly constructed buildings with shapes different from existing ones could be inaccurately delineated; Resolution restrictions of the satellite image limit detection of small protrusions and details

title: Soil Classification and Potentiality Assessment for Some Rainfed Areas at West of Matrouh, Northwestern Coast of Egypt
relevance_reason: The paper is a soil science and agricultural assessment study; the single mention of a 'vector database' refers to a GIS spatial data structure for geographic features, not a vector database for similarity search or nearest neighbor retrieval.
research_focus: Soil classification and agricultural potentiality assessment in the El-Qasr-Um El-Rakham rainfed area on the northwestern coast of Egypt, including identification of landforms, soil types, and suitability for agricultural expansion.
method: Survey of 261 soil profiles spatially distributed over ETM+ LANDSAT 7 image classification, field and laboratory analysis of 24 representative profiles, GIS-based digital vector database creation, and soil classification following Soil Survey Staff (2010) taxonomy.
results_summary: The paper classified soils in the El-Qasr-Um El-Rakham area into 10 family classes and 7 sub-great group classes based on profile depth, texture, and topography. Agricultural potentiality was assessed, with 13.6% of the area rated 'Good,' 19.6% 'Fair,' 22.6% 'Poor,' and the remainder 'Very poor' or 'Non agricultural.' Low potentiality was attributed to limited profile depth, poor drainage, coarse texture, high salinity, high lime content, and low fertility. The study used 261 soil profiles distributed over LANDSAT 7 classified landforms and created a GIS-based digital vector database to generate soil and evaluation maps.

title: A multidisciplinary approach to reveal palaeo-hydrographic features: the case study of Luna archaeological site surroundings
relevance_reason: The 'vector databases' mentioned in this paper are GIS databases for storing geographic vector features (lines and polygons representing river channels and marshy areas), which is an entirely different concept from vector databases for similarity search and nearest neighbor retrieval. The paper is about palaeo-hydrographic analysis using GIS and remote sensing, with no connection to vector indexing, embedding search, or similarity search technology.
research_focus: Identifying and mapping palaeo-hydrographic features (ancient river channels, streams, marshy areas) around the Roman colony of Luna in north-western Italy using a multidisciplinary GIS-based approach combining remote sensing, historical cartography, and field surveys.
method: GIS-based integration of multi-temporal remote sensing data (Landsat 7 ETM+ satellite imagery and high-resolution aerial photos), historical cartography spanning the 16th to 20th centuries, and recent field/stratigraphic surveys to detect, code, and organize palaeo-hydrographic traces into geographic vector databases of linear and polygonal features.
application_domain: Palaeo-hydrography and archaeological landscape analysis
results_summary: The paper combined multi-temporal remote sensing data, historical cartography, and field surveys within a GIS environment to identify palaeo-hydrographic features around the Luna archaeological site. Identified traces were coded as palaeo-fluvial traces or damp areas and organized into GIS vector databases of linear and polygonal geographic features. The best detection results were obtained using the Landsat 7 ETM+ panchromatic band and greylevel high-resolution aerial photos, with filtering and stretching techniques enhancing feature visibility. The findings were consistent with historical cartography and previous geomorphological investigations, revealing ancient river beds, secondary ramifications, and marshy zones. The resulting database provides a preliminary but significant contribution to understanding the landscape evolution of the Magra River alluvial plain.
limitations: The study does not aim to be an exhaustive study of the palaeo-hydrography of the investigated area; In the western sector of Luna, the low number of traces from different source data did not allow an adequately reliable identification of elements; Most elements in the western area were identified only in high-spatial-resolution images, giving them only moderate reliability; The area is difficult to investigate due to the complex geomorphological evolution of the landscape and the impact of land reclamation
research_gaps: Further more detailed studies aimed at better understanding the evolution of the landscape; Investigating the possible relationship between landscape evolution and the history of the archaeological site of Luna, about which many questions are still unresolved

title: A Multidisciplinary GIS-Based Approach for Mapping Paleoriver Migration: A Case Study of the Serchio River (Lucca Alluvial Plain, Tuscany)
relevance_reason: The 'vector database' mentioned in the paper is a GIS spatial database storing geographic line features (paleochannel traces), which is entirely unrelated to vector databases for high-dimensional similarity search or nearest-neighbor retrieval. The paper's subject is paleoriver mapping and geomorphology, not vector database technology.
research_focus: Mapping paleoriver migration of the Serchio River in the Lucca alluvial plain (Tuscany, Italy) using a multidisciplinary GIS-based approach that combines remote sensing, stratigraphic, archaeological, and geomorphological data.
method: Processing remote sensing imagery of different resolution (aerial orthophotos at 1 m and 50 cm, satellite images at 15 m) to enhance buried fluvial features, combined with stratigraphic investigations (penetration tests, boreholes), archaeological surveys, geomorphological maps, and historical cartography, all stored and analyzed in a GIS environment with a georeferenced vector layer of 169 linear features.
application_domain: Paleohydrography and geomorphology (mapping ancient river channels in an alluvial plain)
results_summary: The paper combined remote sensing data of varying resolution with stratigraphic and archaeological data to identify 169 paleochannel traces in the Lucca alluvial plain. Two distinct fluvial channel systems were identified: a primary system (channels >50 m wide, >2.5 km long) comprising two branches (western and eastern) originating north of Antraccoli, and a secondary system (channels <20 m wide, <1.3 km long) with 40 traces possibly linked to Roman-era land reclamation. The results confirmed major features from previous studies and enabled discovery of smaller channels due to higher-resolution aerial orthophotos. All detected features were compiled in a georeferenced GIS vector database with attribute tables recording identification degree, type, hierarchy, length, and municipality. The findings suggest the secondary drainage network was modified by human activity beginning in the Roman period.
limitations: Imperfect match with previous studies (e.g., Cosci 2005) attributed to different spatial resolution of the analyzed images; Difficulty comparing secondary system data with previous studies because the size of investigated fluvial elements is highly variable and a secondary system was often not distinguished in earlier work

title: Real time vector database updating system: a case study for Turkish topographic vector database (Topovt)
relevance_reason: The paper is about a geographic/topographic vector database (storing vector GIS features like points, lines, polygons) and its real-time updating workflow, not about vector databases in the sense of high-dimensional vector storage and similarity/nearest-neighbor search. No vector indexing, embedding search, or similarity search technology is discussed.
research_focus: Design and implementation of a real-time updating system for the Turkish Topographic Vector Database (TOPOVT) to enable governmental institutions and municipalities to share and update geospatial data, avoiding duplicate data production.
method: The paper proposes a web-based real-time updating system using OGC standards (WFS, WMS) that allows multiple governmental institutions to contribute topographic vector data to a central database, with quality assurance mechanisms and a shared data schema for interoperability.
application_domain: Topographic mapping and geospatial data management for national mapping in Turkey
results_summary: The paper presents the design of a real-time updating system for TOPOVT that allows governmental institutions and municipalities to directly access and update the national topographic vector database via the internet. The system aims to eliminate duplicate geospatial data production, reduce costs, and keep the database current through contributions from multiple data producers. Quality assurance is addressed through feature-level metadata, 10% data sampling checks, and periodic revision by the General Command of Mapping. The paper concludes that the main challenge is harmonizing different data formats and models across institutions, and suggests future work on system refinements and incorporating volunteered geographic information (VGI) from citizens.
limitations: Governmental institutions currently gather geospatial data in different formats and models, making interoperability difficult; The mutual will of all stakeholders is the most important factor for the project's success; The system requires an agreed-upon schema for exchanging geospatial data between institutions
research_gaps: Discussing the outputs of the system in further studies; Refinements to the system; Improving the system to allow VGI (volunteered geographic information) from Turkish citizens via mobile phones to contribute observations to a condensed version of TOPOVT

title: An automatic method for road centerline extraction from post-earthquake aerial images
relevance_reason: The paper is about automatic road centerline extraction from post-earthquake aerial images; the 'vector database' mentioned refers to a GIS road network dataset (vector geographic features), not a vector similarity search database, and no vector indexing, nearest neighbor search, or vector database technology is discussed.
research_focus: Automatic road centerline extraction and correction from post-earthquake aerial images, using OpenStreetMap vector road data as a geometric constraint to overcome geo-localization errors in free road datasets.
method: A road centerline correction method that rectifies centerlines using context features and spectral gradient features of post-event aerial images within a circle template, constrained by the OpenStreetMap vector road map, employing a road energy model that considers road homogeneity, spectral features, and morphological gradient.
application_domain: Post-earthquake road network analysis and remote sensing image interpretation
results_summary: The paper proposes an automatic road centerline correction method that uses OpenStreetMap vector data to provide seed points and directions, then rectifies centerlines using context and spectral gradient features in a circle template. Experiments on 0.5 m/pixel post-event aerial images of Haiti 2010 demonstrated completeness over 90% and extraction quality over 80% without manual intervention. The method was compared against two semiautomatic approaches (KDE/mean shift and circle template tracing). The road energy model in the circle template was shown to better handle building collapse, stains, and vehicles on roads.
limitations: Direction errors from the original vector data (OpenStreetMap) can propagate into the extracted centerlines; The method has not been validated across various scenarios with different spatial resolutions
research_gaps: More experiments on various scenarios with different spatial resolution are needed to further prove the method's effectiveness

title: Study on the Effect of Job Accessibility and Residential Location on Housing Occupancy Rate: A Case Study of Xiamen, China
relevance_reason: The paper mentions a 'population spatial vector database' which is a GIS spatial database for geographic data, not a vector database for similarity search or nearest neighbor retrieval. The paper contains no discussion of vector indexing, ANN search, or any vector database technology relevant to the survey.
research_focus: The effect of job accessibility and residential location (under different urban expansion models: concentric zone, sector, and multiple nuclei) on housing occupancy rates in new towns, using Jimei District in Xiamen, China as a case study.
method: OLS regression analysis using a population spatial vector database (GIS) of Jimei District in 2020, with job accessibility calculated via the ELMO model and residential location operationalized through three urban expansion theories.
application_domain: Urban planning and housing policy (spatial analysis of job-housing relationships in new towns)
results_summary: The paper empirically analyzes how job accessibility and residential location under different urban expansion models affect housing occupancy rates in Xiamen's Jimei District. OLS regression results show that job accessibility has a stable positive impact on occupancy rates overall. The concentric zone model residential areas have the highest occupancy, followed by the sector model, with the multiple nuclei model lowest. The interaction effects reveal that sector model areas are highly dependent on job accessibility, while concentric areas show a negative interaction (higher job accessibility associated with lower occupancy), and multiple nuclei areas show no significant effect of job accessibility. The findings suggest that new town planning should prioritize population aggregation strategies and balance industrial agglomeration with job-housing relationships.
limitations: Research scope was limited to Jimei District rather than the whole Xiamen city; The assumption of homogeneity of job opportunities did not involve structural matching between different industries, occupations, and levels of positions; Living preferences are not monitored long-term; changes in working lifestyles (home office, cross-regional collaboration) may affect job-housing preference
research_gaps: Expanding the job search scope to the whole Xiamen city to explore job accessibility between new and old cities and between new urban areas; Investigating the job-housing relationship at different industrial levels to provide specific suggestions on residential block characteristics (price, area, apartment type, floor area ratio); Long-term monitoring of living preferences and how internet-age working lifestyles affect job-housing proximity preference; How to reasonably arrange mixed land use at small scale under the spatial structure of industrial and population agglomeration at the macro level

title: An evaluation of soil retention potential as an important factor of water balance in the landscape
relevance_reason: The paper is about soil water retention capacity and pedotransfer functions; the 'vector database' mentioned is a GIS spatial database storing classified soil-ecological units, not a vector database for embedding similarity search or nearest neighbor search.
research_focus: Estimation of soil water retention capacity (WRC) in Slovakia using pedotransfer functions compatible with a GIS vector database of classified soil-ecological units, with case studies in the Levoča and Hriňová areas.
method: A model algorithm was created from selected soil parameters (particle size, bulk density, organic carbon, morphometric parameters) to be compatible with the GIS vector database of classified soil-ecological units, enabling spatial mapping of the cumulative coefficient of water retention capacity (CWRC).
application_domain: Soil hydrology, land use planning, and flood risk assessment in Slovakia
results_summary: The paper develops a model algorithm for estimating soil water retention capacity using parameters from a GIS vector database of classified soil-ecological units in Slovakia. The model enables spatial identification of flood risk areas and supports land use planning for water management under changing climate conditions.
limitations: Pedotransfer functions are deficient for complex evaluation of soil cover due to disagreements about attributes; Direct measurement of hydrological data for soil is very difficult in terms of capacity; Possibilities to compare simulations with field measurements are limited

title: OpenStreetMap – building data completeness visualization in terms of “Fitness for purpose”

results_summary: The paper assessed OSM building data completeness in Piaseczno County by comparing it with the BDOT10k reference database using three proprietary indices. title: Sea Bottom Classification by Means of Bathymetric LIDAR Data

results_summary: The paper presents a method for classifying sea bottom types using bathymetric LIDAR data in a shallow coastal environment. title: Urban Heat Island mapping based on a Local Climate Zone classification: A case study in Strasbourg city, France

research_focus: Mapping the Urban Heat Island (UHI) effect in Strasbourg using a Local Climate Zone (LCZ) classification derived from a GIS vector database of land cover and cadastral parcel data, combined with fuzzy logic and multiple linear regression.
method: A vector-based GIS approach: LCZ polygons are digitized from cadastral maps, LCZ parameters (including new vegetation and compactness indices) are calculated per polygon, a trapezoidal fuzzy logic model with a decision tree assigns LCZ classes, and a multiple linear regression links LCZ parameters to UHI intensity.
application_domain: Urban climate and GIS-based urban morphology analysis
results_summary: The paper developed a vector-based LCZ classification for Strasbourg using cadastral and land cover data, adding two new parameters (VgSF and CI) beyond the standard six. A multiple linear regression then linked LCZ parameters to UHI intensity, producing a UHI map that captures spatial heterogeneity. The vector-based LCZ map was compared to a raster-based one and found to be similarly relevant but more accurate due to more precise input data. The resulting UHI map was also compared to one produced by the Meso-NH atmospheric model, showing noteworthy similarities.

title: Monthly variation and spatial distribution of quadrant tropical cyclone size in the Western North Pacific

No vector indexing, similarity search, or vector database technology is discussed.
research_focus: Monthly variation and spatial distribution of quadrant tropical cyclone size in the Western North Pacific, including the classification of TCs into symmetric and asymmetric structures and the influence of atmospheric circulation on quadrant size.
method: Analysis of 225 tropical cyclone cases (2000-2009) using QuikSCAT near-surface wind data and a best-track dataset, classifying TCs by symmetry index and examining quadrant size variation by type, season, and spatial region.
application_domain: Meteorology / Tropical cyclone climatology
results_summary: The paper analyzed 1,229 TC size parameters derived from 225 TCs in the Western North Pacific during 2000-2009, classifying them into symmetric and four types of asymmetric structures (NE, SE, SW, NW). Monthly variation of maximum quadrant sizes showed distinct seasonal peaks for each asymmetric type, with NE-type peaking in July and October and SW-type being larger from June to August. Lifetime and background atmospheric circulation were identified as key factors influencing quadrant size, with four circulation patterns correlating with the four asymmetric types. The study also noted that TC track, duration in a region, and overlapping circulation patterns complicate the attribution of quadrant size differences.
limitations: The four specified circulation regions overlap, so two or more kinds of circulation may occur simultaneously, making it difficult to estimate which quadrant size is larger in that situation; A NE-type TC may change to a NW type over time, complicating the analysis of quadrant size evolution
research_gaps: More factors should be discussed in future studies, such as the relative sea surface temperature (SST) and its relationship to TC size; Further studies are planned to consider TC structure in a motion-relative reference frame to better understand asymmetry; The influence of wind shear on TC asymmetry should be examined in a motion-relative reference frame without transition effects

Results showed that natural areas (forests, water reservoirs) consistently received the highest aesthetic scores, while highly urbanised and sealed areas received the lowest. The study demonstrated the feasibility of using open spatial data and GIS tools to build scenario-based aesthetic assessments.
limitations: BDOT10k vector data is updated only on a five-year cycle, limiting timeliness; OSM lacks some object classes needed for aesthetic assessment (e.g. certain barriers/fences); Satellite-derived imperviousness raster data is limited to 2018 timeliness and less reliable in areas of intensive development; Statistical data from the LDB collected for municipalities does not work well in grid-based basic field analyses; No single data source covers all needed information, requiring combination of multiple datasets

research_focus: Integration of SWAT hydrological modelling with Multi-Criteria Decision-Making (MCDM) analysis to assess spatial suitability for small hydropower development in the Rasina River catchment, Serbia.
method: SWAT model for hydrological simulation (water balance, sediment transport, erosion) validated against observed data, combined with a weighted overlay MCDM method in ArcGIS Pro incorporating terrain slope, soil type, land cover, proximity to infrastructure, and ecological impact criteria.
application_domain: spatial planning, hydropower site selection, catchment hydrology
results_summary: The paper applied an integrated SWAT-MCDM framework to the 522 km² Rasina River catchment to identify optimal locations for small hydropower development. title: 3D Modelling of Vegetation from Optical and LiDAR Point Clouds for Inclusion in Basic Nationwide Built Environment Model
relevance_reason: The paper is about 3D vegetation modelling from LiDAR and optical point clouds for geographic information purposes; the phrase 'geographic vector database' refers to a GIS data store (ZABAGED), not a vector database for similarity search or nearest neighbor retrieval.
research_focus: Proposing a compliant workflow for 3D modelling of two vegetation feature types (forests and solitary trees) from optical and LiDAR point clouds for inclusion in the Czech Republic's basic nationwide built environment model under the new BIM Act.
method: Optical point cloud filtration and constrained Delaunay triangulation for forest canopy modelling; individual tree detection and parameter extraction from segmented point clouds for solitary trees; prototype-based implicit geometry with scaling; storage in CityGML/3DCityDB at LoD2 level.
application_domain: 3D built environment modelling, urban forestry, geographic information systems
results_summary: The paper proposes automated workflows for 3D modelling of forests and solitary trees from nationwide datasets. For forests, optical point cloud filtration combined with constrained Delaunay triangulation produced height-extruded base polygons with TIN canopy tops, stored as MultiSurface PlantCover objects in CityGML/3DCityDB. For solitary trees, predefined prototypes were scaled and positioned based on parameters (height, crown diameter) extracted from segmented point clouds, using Implicit geometry. The optical digital surface model proved sufficient for forest features, while aerial laser scanning data was superior for individual tree modelling. The results demonstrate generation of LoD2-compliant 3D models from nationwide datasets, visually enriching the basic built environment model.
limitations: Availability of high-density laser scanning data in Europe is limited and varies significantly across countries and regions; The number of extractable individual tree parameters is dependent on the platform used and point density
